transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-15
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 68 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Elena Soto (Redwood CSM); Liam O'Connor (Stratus Edge HoS), Priya Rao (DevOps), Diego Marquez (AppSec), Hannah Lee (IT Ops)

Summary:
Quick sync to review the recent penetration test findings Stratus ran (third-party), align on vuln triage and prioritization, discuss secure SDLC adjustments and weekly vs monthly patch cadence, and confirm encryption/KMS questions and audit log retention for compliance. Agreed next steps and owners.

Topics:
- Penetration test highlights and risk classification
- Vulnerability management process and SLA for criticals
- Patch cadence (hotfix vs monthly cadence) and deployment gating
- Secure SDLC (SAST/DAST/third-party libs, dependency scanning)
- RBAC/SSO and least-privilege improvements
- Audit logs, retention, and KMS/encryption questions
- SOC 2 / ISO artifacts and evidence requests

Action items (captured): see metadata action_items field above.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, we know you had the pen test back last week so wanted to walk through the findings and then figure out remediation and cadence. Liam do you want to kick us off with context on the scope?
[00:20] Liam O'Connor: yeah thanks Maya. Scope was ex-internal test against our public inference endpoints and internal admin portal, they did authenticated checks for privilege escalation. Third party run by RedRock Security, redacted report sent around, main focus was sqli in an old microservice, some insecure direct object refs, and a couple of misconfigurations on rbac.
[00:45] Ravi Patel: when you say rbac misconfigs can you be specific, like roles too permissive or mis-mapped policies?
[00:54] Priya Rao: mostly roles too broad, service accounts had cluster-admin-ish rights in a couple of dev clusters, and some API keys were stored in cleartext in a legacy repo. The scanner missed a few findings, the human tester found them.
[01:20] Diego Marquez: also an issue with session fixation on the admin UI flows, they could hijack a session id after token refresh in certain corner cases.
[01:35] Maya Chen: ok, thanks. from a Redwood perspective we often see the same class: legacy service accounts, over-broad IAM roles, and then storage of secrets in repos. we can talk through recommended fixes and temporary mitigations like rotating keys and scoping service accounts.
[01:55] Hannah Lee: quick Q on timelines — we usually want to close crits within 72 hours, highs in 14 days, is that kinda the expectation?
[02:06] Ravi Patel: that's a good baseline; we recommend for production inference endpoints critical RTO should be very tight given live traffic, 72 hours for critical with hotfix process, high is usually 7-14 days depending on exploitability. we can propose a triage SLA in the runbook.
[02:35] Liam O'Connor: one of our constraints is Canary traffic — we need to keep latency SLOs stable. hotfixes that increase CPU or change batching can cause ripple effects. how would that work with Redwood Dedicated?
[02:50] Maya Chen: good call. For Dedicated customers you can pin versions and route during canaries; Ravi can cover a recommended canary+rollback pattern that minimizes perf and kvcache impact.
[03:04] Ravi Patel: yes, typically we advise a small canary fleet with mirrored traffic, watch latency percentiles and KV cache hit rates. rollout with automatic rollback on latency bump. but patches that change model artifacts or quantization need more careful staging.
[03:35] Diego Marquez: about KMS — the pen test had a note re: key material exposure in staging. we use AWS KMS in prod, but staging had a self-hosted Vault with lax ACLs. Thoughts on consolidation?
[03:52] Maya Chen: consolidation to a single KMS per environment is best practice. also we recommend using customer-managed keys for sensitive workloads. we do support HSM-backed keys for Private deployments; Elena has the doc link.
[04:10] Elena Soto: I'll share the KMS integration guide and our Private deployment KMS notes after the call.
[04:20] Priya Rao: thanks. for audit logs — how long do you recommend retention? Compliance needs say 1 year for some controls but SOC 2 evidence might require 6 months.
[04:33] Ravi Patel: SOC 2 is typically 6-12 months depending on the control; ISO can require different windows. Our platform stores detailed token-level audit logs and you can export to your SIEM to meet longer retention. We recommend 1 year on-platform + cold archival for 7 years for regulated industries.
[04:55] Liam O'Connor: are the logs tamper-evident? we need chain-of-custody for an audit.
[05:02] Maya Chen: yes we can provide append-only logs with SHA hashes and integration to your log archive. note that some transcript tools mislabel things, but the underlying logs are cryptographically verifiable.
[05:25] Hannah Lee: question re: RBAC improvements — can Redwood integrate with our Okta groups and do attribute-based access?
[05:33] Ravi Patel: we have SAML/SCIM provisioning for Okta and support attribute-based rules. sometimes SCIM mapping to role sets requires a mapping layer, but we can show sample policies.
[05:48] Priya Rao: a weird find in the pen test — some refresh tokens were long lived in staging because the cron job that rotated them failed. could Redwood provide guidance on token lifetime best practices?
[06:03] Ravi Patel: yes, rotate tokens frequently, use short TTLs for refresh tokens in staging and require automatic rotation for service accounts. also leverage prefix KV cache to reduce dependency on long-lived tokens.
[06:26] Diego Marquez: the pen test also flagged dependency vulnerabilities (old jackson libs) — we currently run SCA monthly. should we increase cadence?
[06:35] Maya Chen: for high-risk dependencies we recommend continuous scanning in CI and weekly triage of critical/CVE-0day classes. for medium risk monthly might be OK, but the secure SDLC should include automated blocking thresholds in PR checks for criticals.
[07:00] Priya Rao: ok we'll tighten CI gating.
[07:07] Liam O'Connor: can we walk through one critical finding and remediation steps so we document the ticket?
[07:15] Maya Chen: sure, which one? the SQLi in the public inference microservice?
[07:22] Diego Marquez: yes that one. the tester showed a parameter that wasn't parameterized in one legacy endpoint.
[07:30] Ravi Patel: remediation pattern: 1) immediate mitigation — put a WAF rule to block the vector, 2) patch code to use prepared statements, 3) add SAST rule and a unit test to prevent regression, 4) rollout to canary with traffic mirror, 5) require post-deploy pentest sign-off if the exposure was exploitable.
[07:55] Hannah Lee: WAF will buy us time, we can also rate-limit that endpoint.
[08:02] Maya Chen: good. action owner for that one?
[08:05] Priya Rao: I'll take the WAF and JIRA ticket creation.
[08:09] Maya Chen: great, noted.
[08:12] Liam O'Connor: for vulnerability management — how should we classify exploitability vs impact? RedRock labeled some as high but not exploitable in prod. We want a clear rubric for triage.
[08:26] Ravi Patel: we recommend triage on two axes: exploitability (publicly reachable, authenticated only, requires local access) and impact (data exposure, RCE, privilege escalation). A critical is usually high impact + high exploitability. We can share a spreadsheet rubric.
[08:45] Diego Marquez: when you talk about hotfix vs scheduled patching, how do you measure risk of regressions? we had a bad hotfix once that impacted the kvcache and spiked latency.
[08:58] Maya Chen: mitigations: run canary with mirrored traffic, set rollback triggers on 95/99p latency and error budget, and pre-run synthetic load tests against the canary. Also keep patch changes minimal — separate config-only fixes from code changes that affect batching/runtime.
[09:25] Priya Rao: question on data residency — we've got EU customers and some logs need to be kept in eu-west-1. does Redwood support per-tenant residency?
[09:35] Ravi Patel: yes, we support region-pin for data residency on both Hosted and Dedicated; for Private we can do on-prem. We'll explain the difference between control plane metadata vs tokenized payloads and how to pin.
[09:52] Liam O'Connor: SOC 2 artifacts request — what should we expect to get from Redwood?
[09:58] Elena Soto: standard SOC 2 Type II report, control narratives, and a mapping doc to common security controls. we can't share customer-specific logs but we share the control evidence and how it's implemented.
[10:12] Maya Chen: and on ISO, we have a self-attestation pack + cert for if we're certified; I'll include the checklist.
[10:20] Priya Rao: for patch cadence, what's recommended for infra vs app?
[10:26] Ravi Patel: infra CVEs with active exploits => immediate hotfix. infra patching cadence commonly monthly for non-critical patches; apps we recommend weekly dependency scans and monthly releases for non-critical updates. Critical app bugs follow the hotfix path.
[10:45] Diego Marquez: ok. can Redwood help with triage during our sprint planning so engineering isn't overwhelmed?
[10:52] Elena Soto: yes our CSM can help prioritize and run the first 2-3 sprints with you, help set up dashboards and runbook items. we often co-author the remediation backlog in early engagements.
[11:05] Liam O'Connor: good. on evidence retention for audits — what's the default retention for audit logs?
[11:12] Ravi Patel: default is 90 days on the console, exportable to S3 for longer retention. can be configured to ship to your SIEM (Splunk, Datadog indexes, etc.) for the timeframe you need.
[11:28] Hannah Lee: odd question — the pen test report uses a vendor name that transcription sometimes garbles (they said RedRock but sometimes shows RedDock). just flagging transcription quirks.
[11:38] Maya Chen: yes noted, we'll attach the PDF to the CRM and not rely on transcript names.
[11:45] Priya Rao: curious about RBAC labels: can we have ephemeral admin for debugging, like 1-hour elevation?
[11:52] Ravi Patel: yes ephemeral elevation via SSO claims is supported; tie it to audit logs and require justification. We can show sample Okta workflow.
[12:08] Diego Marquez: any recommendations for secrets in repos? we already moved to a secrets manager but legacy repos still have tokens.
[12:15] Maya Chen: sweep legacy repos with SCA or git-secrets, rotate any exposed tokens, and enforce pre-commit hooks. Also add automated alerts for new secrets in PRs.
[12:33] Liam O'Connor: final recap and owners?
[12:38] Maya Chen: recap: Maya will send redacted pen-test and exec summary; Ravi will draft remediation runbook and canary/rollback recommendations; Priya will create JIRA epic and tickets; Elena will send SOC2/ISO artifacts. We'll meet again for a 30-min remediation plan week of Oct 26.
[12:58] Priya Rao: thanks everyone, that works.
[13:05] Maya Chen: perfect, thanks all, we'll follow up in email and add the docs to the CRM.
[68:00] End of meeting

Notes on transcription: contains occasional mislabels and minor transcription errors (e.g., RedRock vs RedDock, KV cache sometimes spelled K V cache). Some technical terms shortened in speech (SAML/SCIM pronounced quickly). The action items and next steps above reflect agreed owners and due dates.
